entry: Length of an organism's life, especially exceptional longevity in humans. [[Life expectancy]], the average number of years remaining at a given age, is a statistical measure distinct from longevity, which refers to especially long-lived members of a population. In developed countries life expectancy ranges from 77–90 years; in developing countries, from 32–80 years. Canada's was 81.29 years (2010 est.) and Mozambique's 41.37 years. Significant factors in life expectancy include gender, [[Genetics|genetics]], access to [[Health care|health care]], hygiene, diet and nutrition, exercise, and crime rates. Twin studies estimate that 20–30% of the variation in human lifespan relates to genetics. The oldest person whose age has been verified by modern documentation was [[Jeanne Calment]], who lived 122 years and 164 days. Jiroemon Kimura, who lived 116 years and 54 days, is the oldest man so verified. The Gerontology Research Group validates records and maintains a list of [[Supercentenarian|supercentenarians]].

East-west geographic coordinate of a point on the surface of Earth or another celestial body. Longitude is an angular measurement, usually expressed in degrees and denoted by the Greek letter lambda (λ). The [[Prime meridian]] defines 0° longitude; by convention it passes near the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, England, and positive longitudes lie east of it. Because of [[Earth's rotation]], a difference of 15° of longitude corresponds to a one-hour difference in local time, so longitude can be found by comparing local time with an absolute time. [[Hipparchus]], in the 2nd century BC, divided the spherical Earth into 360° and proposed comparing the local time of a [[Lunar eclipse|lunar eclipse]] observed at two places. Determining longitude at sea was a central problem until clockmaker John Harrison's marine chronometers; his H4 model, tested in 1761–1762, lost only seconds over months-long voyages. Unlike [[Latitude|latitude]] lines, meridians converge at the poles.

Largest settlement and administrative center of [[Svalbard]], Norway, and one of the world's northernmost settlements. Its population is estimated at 2,400–2,800. Coal mining began in 1906 under the [[Boston]]-based Arctic Coal Company, of which American John Munro Longyear was a main shareholder; the town was known as Longyear City until 1926. Store Norske Spitsbergen Kulkompani took over the mining in 1916, and production ceased in 2017. The German Kriegsmarine almost completely destroyed the town on 8 September 1943. The town hosts the Svalbard Global Seed Vault. Burials are restricted because [[Permafrost|permafrost]] inhibits [[Decomposition|decomposition]]. As of 2021, Longyearbyen was the fastest-warming town in the world.

Device for [[Weaving|weaving]] cloth and [[Tapestry|tapestry]]. The basic purpose of any loom is to hold warp threads under tension so that weft threads can be interlaced with them. The earliest looms, dating from the 5th millennium BC, were bars or beams fixed in place to hold parallel threads in tension. Weaving requires three principal motions. Shedding separates the warp threads to form a shed through which the shuttle carries the weft; picking passes the weft through the shed; and battening compresses each new weft thread against the fell. Conventional shuttle looms run at about 150 to 160 picks per minute. Take-up and let-off motions wind the finished cloth onto the cloth beam and release warp from the warp beam. An automatic loom requires 0.125 hp to 0.5 hp (100W to 400W). The word derives from the [[Old English]] *geloma*, a term for a utensil, tool or machine of any kind.

Aquatic diving bird of the family Gaviidae, found in much of North America and northern Eurasia, known as a diver in British and Irish English. All living loons belong to the genus *Gavia* and order Gaviiformes. Loons are the size of large [[Duck|ducks]] or small geese, with webbed feet, a spear-shaped bill and largely black-and-white summer plumage. Their feet are set far back on the body, making them strong swimmers but awkward on land. Most species must run across the water to take off; only the red-throated loon (*G. stellata*) can take off from land. Satellite-tracked loons have flown up to 1,078 km (670 mi) in 24 hours. Loons can live as long as 30 years and hold their breath for as long as 90 seconds underwater. In winter they move from northern freshwater lakes to southern marine coastlines, where salt glands above the eyes filter salts from the blood.

American animated short-film series and media franchise owned by Warner Bros. Entertainment. The series of animated shorts ran from 1930 to 1969, alongside its spin-off *Merrie Melodies*, and was revived in the late 1970s. Its characters include [[Bugs Bunny]], [[Daffy Duck]] and Porky Pig. The title was inspired by [[Walt Disney|Walt Disney]]'s *Silly Symphonies*. Bugs Bunny became popular in the *Merrie Melodies* shorts of the early 1940s, and the series moved to color between 1942 and 1943. From 1942 to 1964 they were the most popular animated shorts in movie theaters. Directors including Tex Avery, Chuck Jones and Bob Clampett shaped the shorts, and voice actor [[Mel Blanc]] was central to them. Five films won Academy Awards. In 2013, TV Guide ranked the series third among television cartoons, behind [[The Simpsons]] and [[The Flintstones]]. Bugs Bunny, the Warner Bros. mascot, has a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Indiscriminate taking of goods by force, typically during war, [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]] or [[Riot|riots]]. Its proceeds are called booty, loot, plunder, spoils or pillage, and looting occurs when law and civil enforcement are temporarily ineffective. Looting by victorious armies was long considered a customary right until norms against wartime plunder became widely accepted after the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and especially after [[World War II]]. Modern armed conflicts prohibit it under international law, and it constitutes a [[War crime|war crime]]; the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 explicitly prohibited pillage and looting. Disaster researchers have found that post-disaster looting is often cooperative rather than criminal, and that reports of mass looting after [[Hurricane Katrina]] were often inaccurate or overstated. Scholars argue that such narratives can reinforce stereotypes; media coverage after Katrina more often labeled Black residents as "looters" than white residents, who were described as "finding" supplies.

Spanish playwright, poet and novelist, a key figure of the Spanish Golden Age of Baroque literature. Born in [[Madrid]], he renewed Spanish theater when it became mass culture. With [[Pedro Calderón de la Barca]] and Tirso de Molina, he defined the characteristics of Spanish Baroque theater, with great insight into the human condition. His output includes some 3,000 [[Sonnet|sonnets]], three novels, four novellas, nine epic poems and approximately 500 stageplays. [[Miguel de Cervantes]] called him "The Phoenix of Wits" (*Fénix de los ingenios*), and the volume of his work earned him the envy of contemporaries such as Cervantes and Luis de Góngora. He was a friend of the writer Francisco de Quevedo and an enemy of the dramatist Juan Ruiz de Alarcón. [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]] admired his vast and colorful oeuvre.

British Romantic poet, regarded as among the greatest British poets. Educated at [[University of Cambridge|Trinity College at the University of Cambridge]], he traveled extensively in Europe and lived for seven years in Italy, in [[Venice]], Ravenna, Pisa and Genoa, after being forced to flee England amid threats of lynching. His best-known works are the lengthy narratives *Childe Harold's Pilgrimage* and *Don Juan*; his shorter lyrics in *Hebrew Melodies* also became popular. He was a friend of [[Percy Bysshe Shelley]]. Later he joined the [[Greek War of Independence]] against the [[Ottoman Empire]], and Greeks revere him as a folk hero. He died leading a campaign, from a fever contracted after the first and second sieges of Missolonghi.

British mathematician, mathematical physicist and engineer, 1st Baron Kelvin. Born in [[Belfast]], he was professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of [[Glasgow]] for 53 years, researching the mathematical analysis of electricity and helping formulate the first and second laws of [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]]. He determined the correct value of [[Absolute zero]] as approximately −273.15 degrees Celsius or −459.67 degrees Fahrenheit, and absolute temperatures are stated in [[Kelvin|kelvin]] in his honor. He was knighted in 1866 for his work on the transatlantic telegraph, and in 1892 became the first scientist elevated to the House of Lords, honored for his work in thermodynamics and his opposition to Irish Home Rule. His estimate of Earth's age, 20 to 400 million years, underestimated geological timescales because it omitted internal heat sources such as radioactivity, and it sparked debates with [[Charles Darwin]], who required longer periods for evolution.

British statesman and admiral, last viceroy of British India. He served in the [[Royal Navy]] in both world wars and as Supreme Allied Commander, South East Asia, in the Second World War. As viceroy he oversaw the transition to independence and the [[Partition of India|partition]] of British India into the Dominions of India and Pakistan. He later served as First Sea Lord and, until 1965, as Chief of the Defence Staff. Critics accused him of vanity and flawed judgment, particularly over partition. He was assassinated by the Provisional Irish Republican Army when a bomb exploded aboard his fishing boat off Mullaghmore, County Sligo.

Novel by British author William Golding, published in 1954 as his first novel. British boys in middle childhood or preadolescence are stranded on an uninhabited island after a wartime evacuation, and their attempts to govern themselves lead to a descent into savagery. Its themes include [[Morality|morality]], leadership and the tension between civility and chaos. Golding had been a [[Royal Navy|Royal Navy]] lieutenant who commanded a landing craft in the [[Normandy landings]] on D-Day in 1944. Many publishers rejected the manuscript before Faber & Faber accepted it. The title is a literal translation of Beelzebub, a biblical demon considered the god of pride and warfare.

Central Christian prayer attributed to [[Jesus]], also known by its Latin incipit *Pater Noster*. It appears in the [[New Testament|New Testament]] Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and most scholars regard it as deriving authentically from the historical Jesus. The prayer survives in two versions, and the relationship between the Matthean and Lukan forms remains debated. The first-century *Didache* reports a version closely resembling Matthew's, ending with the Minor Doxology. Matthew's version has seven petitions, the first three addressed to God, and it alone includes a petition for God's will to be done. Most [[Christian denomination|Christian denominations]] use the Matthean form, and the prayer has been set to music, from 9th-century [[Gregorian chant]] onward. Since the 16th century it has been widely translated. It shares parallels with the [[Hebrew Bible]] and with texts such as the [[Dhammapada]] and the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]].

New Zealand singer-songwriter, born Ella Marija Lani Yelich-O'Connor, known for an unconventional production style and introspective songwriting in alternative pop. After signing with [[Universal Music Group]], her debut single "Royals" topped the Billboard Hot 100, won two [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], and became one of the best-selling singles of all time. Her album *Pure Heroine* (2013) was followed by *Melodrama* (2017), which debuted atop the US Billboard 200 and was ranked among the "500 Greatest Albums of All Time" by [[Rolling Stone]]. *Solar Power* (2021) explored indie folk and psychedelic styles, and *Virgin* (2025) returned to electronic sounds.

Placeholder text used in publishing and graphic design. Lorem ipsum is typically a corrupted version of *De finibus bonorum et malorum*, a 1st-century BC text by the Roman statesman and philosopher [[Cicero]], with words altered, added and removed to make it nonsensical [[Latin|Latin]]. The first two words are a truncation of *dolorem ipsum* ("pain itself"). Its purpose is to let a page layout be designed independently of the copy that will fill it. Letraset transfer sheets popularized it in the late 1960s, and it was later adopted by [[Microsoft Word]] and by [[CSS]] libraries such as Semantic UI.

Force exerted on a charged particle by electric and magnetic fields. The electric component acts along the electric field, accelerating positive charges in its direction and negative charges opposite to it. The magnetic component is perpendicular to both the particle's velocity and the magnetic field, so it curves the particle's path, often into circles or helices. Together with [[Maxwell's equations]], the force law forms the foundation of classical [[Electromagnetism|electrodynamics]]. It underlies the operation of [[Electric motor|electric motors]], [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerators]] and the behavior of [[Plasma (physics)|plasmas]]. The law remains valid in [[Special relativity|special relativity]] but breaks down at small scales, where the intrinsic spin of particles gives rise to interactions it does not account for. [[Hendrik Lorentz]] completed the derivation in 1895, identifying the electric force a few years after Oliver Heaviside identified the magnetic force. Historians suggest the law is implicit in a paper by [[James Clerk Maxwell|James Clerk Maxwell]] published in 1865.

Linear transformation between the space and time coordinates of two inertial frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other. Named after the Dutch physicist [[Hendrik Lorentz]], the transformations use the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), where v is relative velocity and c is the [[Speed of light|speed of light]]. For motion along the x-axis, t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) and x′ = γ(x − vt), while y and z are unchanged. They supersede the Galilean transformation of Newtonian physics, which is a good approximation only at speeds much less than the speed of light. The transformations predict effects such as [[Time dilation|time dilation]] and length contraction; observers in different frames may measure different distances and elapsed times, yet the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames. [[Albert Einstein]] made them a cornerstone of [[Special relativity|special relativity]].

Florentine statesman, de facto ruler of [[Florence]] from 1469 until his death, known as Lorenzo the Magnificent. The most powerful patron of [[Renaissance]] culture, he sponsored artists including [[Sandro Botticelli|Botticelli]] and [[Michelangelo]]. Lorenzo held the balance of power in the Italic League, an alliance that stabilized the Italian Peninsula for decades. He was the grandson of [[Cosimo de' Medici|Cosimo de' Medici]], who had led the Republic of Florence and run the Medici Bank. Lorenzo ruled indirectly through surrogates in the city councils, by means of payoffs and strategic marriages. He survived the Pazzi conspiracy (1478), in which his brother Giuliano was assassinated. The Peace of Lodi of 1454, which he supported, collapsed with his death. He is buried in the Medici Chapel in Florence.

Largest family of [[Catfish|catfish]] (order Siluriformes), with over 90 genera and just over 680 species. Armored, or suckermouth, catfishes whose bodies are covered in bony plates, they are native to freshwater habitats from [[Costa Rica]] and [[Panama]] through tropical and subtropical [[South America]]. Several genera are sold as "plecos", notably the suckermouth catfish *Hypostomus plecostomus*, and are popular in the [[Aquarium|aquarium]] trade. Most species are herbivores or detritivores, eating [[Algae|algae]], plant matter and microorganisms from biofilms. The largest subfamily, Hypostominae, comprises five tribes. Loricariid [[Fossil|fossils]] are extremely rare; the earliest definitive taxon is *Taubateia*, from the Late Oligocene–Early Miocene of Brazil.

Canadian and American television producer, creator of [[Saturday Night Live]]. Born Lorne David Lipowitz in [[Toronto]], he adopted the surname Michaels early in his career. [[Lily Tomlin]] hired him to produce specials, and he credits that work for [[NBC]] hiring him to create the show. In 1975 he created NBC's *Saturday Night*, renamed *Saturday Night Live* in 1977. He later produced the show again from 1985, and he also produced *Late Night* and *The Kids in the Hall*. He has received 24 Primetime Emmy Awards from 112 nominations, the record for the most nominated individual in the award's history.

[[Major League Baseball|Major League Baseball]] franchise based in [[Los Angeles]], in the National League West division. Founded in 1883 in [[Brooklyn]], the club became the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1932 and moved to Los Angeles before the 1958 season, playing at Dodger Stadium from 1962. The Dodgers have won nine [[World Series]] championships and a record 26 National League pennants. The club broke baseball's color line in 1947 with the debut of [[Jackie Robinson]]. After signing [[Shohei Ohtani]] in December 2023, the Dodgers won consecutive World Series titles in 2024 and 2025.

[[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association]] team based in [[Los Angeles]], California. The franchise began in 1946 as the Detroit Gems and later moved to Minneapolis, winning the 1948 NBL championship, before moving to Los Angeles before the 1960–61 season. The Lakers have won 17 NBA championships, second to the [[Boston Celtics]], and their 33-game winning streak in 1971–72 is the league's longest. Stars including [[Kareem Abdul-Jabbar]], [[Magic Johnson]], [[Kobe Bryant]], [[Shaquille O'Neal]] and [[LeBron James]] led title teams in the 1980s, in 2000–02 and in 2020. Jerry Buss bought the team in 1979 and pioneered basketball as entertainment as well as sport.

Most populous city in [[California|California]] and second-most populous in the United States (pop., 2025: 3.87 million). It is the commercial, financial and cultural center of [[Southern California]]. Its metropolitan area had 12.9 million people in 2024. The city was founded on September 4, 1781, by 44 settlers as El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles. It became part of the United States through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848, at the end of the [[Mexican–American War]], and was incorporated on April 4, 1850. The city is one of the largest hubs of film and television production and has one of the busiest container ports in the Americas. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, and will host them in 2028. Downtown contains the world's largest showcase of architecture designed by [[Frank Gehry]].

Pseudohistorical myth of the [[American Civil War|American Civil War]] holding that the Confederate cause was morally just and not centered on slavery. First articulated in 1866 by journalist Edward A. Pollard in *The Lost Cause: A New Southern History of the War of the Confederates*, it blamed states' rights and Northern aggression for the war. Its proponents built Confederate monuments and wrote history textbooks. The myth peaked at the turn of the 20th century and again during the [[Civil rights movement]] of the 1950s and 1960s. Critics argue that it sustained [[White supremacy|white supremacist]] policies such as Jim Crow laws.

Demographic cohort born from 1883 to 1900, who came of age around [[World War I]]. The term also denotes American expatriate writers living in Paris in the 1920s, including [[Ernest Hemingway|Hemingway]] and [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]]. Gertrude Stein is credited with coining it, and Hemingway popularized it as the epigraph of *The Sun Also Rises* (1926). "Lost" refers to the "disoriented, wandering, directionless" spirit of the war's survivors. Mobilized for World War I, the cohort became the driving force behind cultural changes in major cities during the [[Roaring Twenties]]. Later it endured the [[Great Depression]]. The last known member, Nabi Tajima, reached the age of 117.
